FBC: mild lymphocytosis (4.8 x10⁹/L), CRP 14 — consistent with resolving viral illness. Monospot test ordered. Patient counselled that reactive lymphadenopathy following viral URTI is extremely common at her age. However, given ongoing anxiety, arranged ultrasound of right axilla in four weeks if node not resolved. If node persists beyond six weeks total, to return for reassessment and possible core biopsy discussion. No medications prescribed. Safety net given for enlarging node, new nodes elsewhere, fevers, or night sweats.

72F presenting with three months of lower back pain radiating into her left buttock, attributed by her GP to degenerative lumbar disease — she has a known L4/L5 disc bulge on imaging from two years ago. However, she now reports the pain has changed in character, is present at rest, wakes her at night, and is not relieved by paracetamol or naproxen. Has lost approximately 5kg over three months, attributing it to reduced appetite from pain. She denies bowel or bladder symptoms. PMH: post-menopausal, osteoporosis (on alendronate 70mg weekly and calcium/vitamin D), hypercholesterolaemia. Vitals: BP 146/88, HR 80, afebrile. Exam: tenderness on percussion over L3–L4 spinous processes, mildly reduced range of lumbar movement. No neurological deficit in lower limbs. Bloods: ESR 74, CRP 38, ALP elevated at 198, calcium 2.61 (mildly elevated), protein electrophoresis pending. Hb 104, MCV 88. X-ray lumbar spine: mild degenerative changes only, no obvious lytic lesions, but plain X-ray is insensitive. Given constitutional symptoms, night pain, and elevated inflammatory markers with hypercalcaemia, urgent MRI lumbar spine and bone scan arranged. Haematology referral placed. The clinical picture could represent accelerated degenerative disease, osteoporotic fracture, or something requiring further exclusion. Alendronate held pending further workup.

55M with a six-week history of a hoarse voice and intermittent throat clearing. He initially attributed it to a cold that "never quite went away." He is a current smoker (35 pack-years) and works as a teacher. No dysphagia, no stridor, no haemoptysis. On exam, no cervical lymphadenopathy, no neck mass. Oropharynx appears unremarkable on inspection. Vitals normal. He was treated empirically by his GP with a course of antibiotics for suspected sinusitis with post-nasal drip. Symptoms unchanged. Nasal endoscopy not yet performed. Laryngoscopy arranged via ENT referral — report pending. CXR: no hilar enlargement, no parenchymal mass. The combination of persistent hoarseness beyond four weeks in a heavy smoker necessitates visualisation of the larynx and vocal cords regardless of the likely benign aetiology (vocal cord nodules given voice use as a teacher are highly plausible). Patient advised firmly to stop smoking and given referral to smoking cessation service. Ibuprofen for throat discomfort and vocal hygiene advice given. Return before ENT appointment if dysphagia or stridor develops.

48F known to have Crohn's disease, diagnosed age 22, with predominantly ileocolonic involvement. She presents today with a six-week flare of increased stool frequency (6–8 times daily), cramping abdominal pain, and one episode of PR bleeding. She has had similar flares in the past. Currently on azathioprine 2mg/kg and mesalazine 2.4g/day. On exam: mild diffuse tenderness in the right iliac fossa, no peritonism, no palpable mass. Temp 37.6, HR 94, BP 112/70, weight 54kg (down from 57kg). CRP 62, ESR 88, Hb 101 (normocytic), albumin 31, faecal calprotectin >1800 µg/g. Colonoscopy is overdue — last performed 8 years ago, patient had declined previous surveillance offers. Given the severity of the current flare and the fact that this patient is now approaching 26 years of total disease duration with extensive colonic involvement, surveillance colonoscopy is essential and clinically urgent — both for flare assessment and dysplasia surveillance. Prednisolone 40mg daily started for acute flare management. Azathioprine levels and TPMT status to be rechecked. Gastroenterology notified. Colonoscopy arranged within four weeks.

34M presenting with a two-month history of a firm, non-tender lump on the left side of his neck, posterior triangle. He had an upper respiratory tract infection approximately three weeks prior to noticing it, which has since resolved. The lump has not shrunk. He denies fevers, night sweats, or weight loss. No itching. PMH: nil significant, no regular medications, non-smoker, occasional alcohol. Lives with a cat. On exam: a 2.5cm firm, rubbery, non-tender lymph node in the posterior cervical triangle. No other palpable nodes. No hepatosplenomegaly. Tonsils normal. Oral cavity normal. Skin normal. Vitals: temp 36.7, all observations within normal limits. Bloods: FBC mildly abnormal — lymphocytes 5.2, monocytes elevated at 1.1. CRP mildly elevated at 18. Toxoplasma serology sent, EBV IgG positive (consistent with past infection), CMV IgG positive. Bartonella serology pending given cat exposure. USS neck: hypoechoic lymph node, 26mm, fatty hilum preserved — features leaning toward reactive. However, persistence beyond six weeks with no identifiable infection and in a posterior triangle location cannot be attributed to reactive change without adequate follow-up. Review in three weeks — if no reduction in size, to discuss CT neck/chest/abdomen and ENT or haematology referral.

61F presenting with months of increasing fatigue, intermittent low-grade fevers, and a persistent non-productive cough. She attributes symptoms to post-COVID fatigue — she had a confirmed COVID infection 14 months ago. PMH: hypertension (ramipril 5mg), mild asthma (salbutamol PRN, no preventer). Non-smoker. Works as a librarian. No travel outside of the UK in five years. On exam: mildly reduced air entry at both bases, no wheeze, no crackles. Mild bilateral hilar fullness on CXR — formal report: "bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, differential includes sarcoidosis, lymphoma, or less likely primary tuberculosis." No palpable peripheral lymphadenopathy. Serum ACE: 98 U/L (elevated). Calcium 2.67 (mildly elevated). 24-hour urine calcium elevated. LDH 312 (mildly elevated — non-specific). CT chest with contrast arranged urgently. Pulmonology and haematology referrals placed in parallel. Salbutamol and ramipril continued. Patient advised that while sarcoidosis is the most statistically probable explanation for this picture, the LDH elevation and lymphadenopathy pattern must be fully characterised before treatment is initiated.

52M presenting with a three-month history of vague upper abdominal discomfort and what he describes as "indigestion" not responding to over-the-counter antacids. He also reports feeling full very quickly when eating. No vomiting, no melaena, no dysphagia. He lost 4kg over this period, which he ascribes to eating smaller portions due to the discomfort. PMH: H. pylori treated and eradicated six years ago (confirmed by breath test), no prior endoscopy. Drinks approximately 20 units of alcohol per week. BMI 27. Family history: father died of "stomach problems" — nature unclear. Vitals: BP 130/82, HR 76, afebrile. On examination, mild epigastric tenderness, no mass palpable, no hepatomegaly. Hb 112, MCV low, ferritin 10. CRP 9. Urgent two-week-wait endoscopy referral placed. Commenced on pantoprazole 40mg OD empirically. Patient advised alcohol reduction. The combination of early satiety, unexplained weight loss, iron deficiency, family history, and prior H. pylori infection places this patient in a higher risk group for upper GI pathology. Return urgently if haematemesis or melaena.

38F with a 10-week history of irregular menstrual bleeding — periods now occurring every 2–3 weeks rather than every 5 weeks as was her normal pattern. Spotting between periods on four occasions. No intermenstrual bleeding prior to this. No post-coital bleeding. No pelvic pain. She had a normal smear 18 months ago. PMH: polycystic ovarian syndrome (managed conservatively), obesity (BMI 41), type 2 diabetes (metformin 1g BD). She has never been pregnant. She describes her cycles as historically irregular due to PCOS. On exam: uterus mildly bulky on bimanual, no adnexal masses, cervix appears normal visually. Vitals normal. Transvaginal USS: endometrial thickness 13mm in a premenopausal patient — borderline; technically abnormal in a post-menopausal woman but less definitive here. Ongoing anovulatory cycles from PCOS are a plausible explanation for the irregular bleeding. However, her obesity, diabetes, and anovulatory state represent significant endometrial cancer risk factors even at 38. Endometrial biopsy (Pipelle) arranged. CA-125 pending (non-specific but baseline value useful). Metformin continued. Discussed with gynae: agreed biopsy before any hormonal manipulation.

66M with a four-week history of haematuria — one episode of frank haematuria and two subsequent episodes of pink-tinged urine. No dysuria. No loin pain. No urinary frequency. No weight loss. PMH: well-controlled hypertension (lisinopril 10mg), ex-smoker (20 pack-years, quit 10 years ago). Vitals normal. MSU: no growth, no casts, trace blood on dipstick. Creatinine 88, eGFR 78. PSA 1.8. On examination: no abdominal masses, kidneys not palpable, no bladder tenderness. Painless haematuria in a male ex-smoker over 60 is a bladder cancer red flag until proven otherwise regardless of the absence of other symptoms. Urgent two-week-wait flexible cystoscopy and upper tract imaging (CT urogram) arranged. Lisinopril continued. Patient educated that the most likely cause may be benign (e.g. benign urological lesion, stone, or prostatic bleeding) but that cystoscopy is mandatory and non-negotiable given the clinical profile.

44F with a two-week history of persistent headaches, worse in the morning and associated with one episode of vomiting on waking. She attributes them to tension headaches from work stress — she is a project manager going through a difficult period at work. No visual changes reported, though on direct questioning she reports one episode of "blurry vision" lasting a few seconds last week which she had not volunteered. No focal neurological symptoms. No fever. PMH: migraines with aura in her 20s (resolved), OCP (combined pill), BMI 26. Vitals: BP 138/84, HR 80. Neuro exam: fundoscopy — bilateral papilloedema, subtle but present. GCS 15. No focal motor or sensory deficit. Cranial nerves intact. Given papilloedema, patient referred directly to the emergency department with urgent CT head and neuro review. The OCP was held pending further assessment. Instructed to go directly without delay. The morning predominance, vomiting, and papilloedema suggest raised intracranial pressure — differential is broad and includes idiopathic intracranial hypertension (given BMI and OCP), venous sinus thrombosis, or space-occupying lesion. No diagnosis made at this visit.

71M presenting with a gradually worsening dry cough of four months' duration and mild exertional dyspnoea. He attributes it to "getting older." Ex-smoker — 40 pack-years, quit 15 years ago. No haemoptysis. No weight loss volunteered, but he has lost 3.5kg according to his notes (he was unaware). PMH: COPD (on tiotropium 18mcg daily, salbutamol PRN), previous TB treated and cleared 25 years ago (documented sputum conversion). On amlodipine 5mg and aspirin 75mg. Vitals: O2 sats 93% on air (baseline per notes was 95% six months ago). CXR: new right upper lobe opacification with irregular margins overlying an area of prior TB scarring. CT chest arranged — flagged as urgent. Spirometry: FEV1/FVC 0.58, consistent with COPD. The new CXR opacity is at the site of prior TB scarring, which represents a well-recognised risk site for post-primary lung carcinoma (scar carcinoma) as well as reactivation TB. Sputum AFB x3 sent. Respiratory consultant referral placed. Tiotropium, salbutamol, aspirin, and amlodipine continued. COPD review otherwise deferred pending respiratory outpatient appointment.

50F with a three-month history of altered bowel habit — stools looser than usual, some urgency, and on two occasions she noticed a small amount of blood mixed in. She is attributing this to haemorrhoids, which she has had intermittently for years. No weight loss reported (weight stable at 68kg). No abdominal pain at rest. She takes ibuprofen regularly for chronic lower back pain. PMH: IBS (diagnosed in her 30s), hypertension (amlodipine 5mg). Family history: mother with colorectal cancer diagnosed age 72. On exam: no abdominal masses, mild tenderness in the left iliac fossa. PR exam: small external haemorrhoids present, trace blood on glove. FBC: Hb 118 (borderline low), MCV 81. CRP 22. Faecal immunochemical test (FIT) result: 28 µg Hb/g faeces (above threshold of 10 in this lab). Given FIT positivity, age 50, change in bowel habit, and family history of CRC, two-week-wait colonoscopy referral placed. Ibuprofen changed to paracetamol (to reduce GI bleeding confound and mucosal irritation). Patient counselled that haemorrhoids are likely contributing but a positive FIT requires exclusion of other pathology regardless.

63F with a 5-week history of progressive fatigue, pallor, and mild shortness of breath on exertion. She also reports vague upper abdominal discomfort and early satiety. No overt bleeding noticed. PMH: atrial fibrillation (on apixaban 5mg BD and bisoprolol 2.5mg), type 2 diabetes (metformin 500mg BD). Vitals: BP 122/74, HR 88 and irregular, O2 sats 96%. On exam: pale conjunctivae, mild splenomegaly approximately 2cm below the costal margin. No palpable lymphadenopathy. No hepatomegaly. Hb 79 (normocytic normochromic), MCV 90, WBC 14.2 — differential showing elevated lymphocytes at 9.8, some atypical forms noted on film. Platelets 98. Reticulocyte count low. LDH 490. Uric acid elevated. Peripheral blood film reported by haematologist as: "possible lymphoproliferative disorder — recommend urgent flow cytometry and haematology review." Apixaban and bisoprolol continued. Metformin held given planned CT contrast investigation. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and flow cytometry of peripheral blood arranged. Haematology seen same day. The degree of cytopenia, splenomegaly, and atypical lymphocytes on film require urgent characterisation.

47M presenting with a two-month history of right-sided scrotal heaviness and mild dull aching in the right testis. He initially assumed it was a muscle strain from increased gym activity. He denies acute pain. On exam: right testicle mildly enlarged compared to left, a firm area felt at the upper pole — non-tender. No transillumination of the firm area. Left testis normal. No inguinal lymphadenopathy. No gynaecomastia. Vitals normal. Scrotal USS arranged urgently and performed same day: right testis 4.3 x 3.1cm (enlarged), heterogeneous echogenicity in upper pole with a 1.6cm hypoechoic lesion — no definitive benign features. Tumour markers pending: AFP, beta-hCG, LDH. The ultrasound finding of a heterogeneous intratesticular lesion is presumed testicular malignancy until proven otherwise and urology has been contacted. Urgent urology appointment next morning. Patient advised to avoid any further trauma to the area. No analgesia beyond paracetamol PRN. Patient visibly anxious — time spent counselling him that staging and definitive diagnosis are not yet complete and that treatment outcomes in this tumour type are generally very favourable even if malignancy is confirmed.

69F presents with worsening generalised bone pain over four months, particularly in her ribs and lower back. She was assessed six weeks ago and commenced on codeine 30mg QDS and naproxen 500mg BD for presumed musculoskeletal pain and osteoarthritis. She returns today saying the pain is worse and is waking her at night. She is also increasingly fatigued and reports recurrent infections — two chest infections in three months, both requiring antibiotics. PMH: type 2 diabetes, well-controlled. Vitals: afebrile, BP 136/80, HR 84. On exam: diffuse bony tenderness on palpation of sternum and thoracic spine, no focal neurological deficit. Labs: Hb 93 (normocytic), creatinine 164 (up from 112 six months ago), calcium 2.88 (elevated), total protein markedly elevated at 108 g/L, albumin 38 (so globulin gap greatly elevated at 70). ESR 112. X-ray spine/pelvis: multiple small lytic "punched out" lesions in the skull and pelvis. Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation ordered urgently. Urine Bence Jones protein sent. Haematology urgent referral placed. Codeine continued for pain management. Naproxen held given renal impairment. Adequate hydration advised. The constellation of hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia, bone pain with lytic lesions, and markedly elevated globulins in this age group is highly suggestive of plasma cell dyscrasia.

41M presenting with a six-week history of intermittent painless rectal bleeding, bright red, noticed on wiping. He reports no change in bowel habit, no abdominal pain, no weight loss. He is physically active and eats a high-fibre diet. He has no family history of bowel cancer. PMH: nil. BMI 23. On examination: anoscopy in clinic reveals grade II internal haemorrhoids with mild mucosal prolapse — these are actively bleeding on contact. PR exam: no palpable rectal mass, no induration. FBC: Hb 138, normal MCV. CRP 4. FIT test: 4 µg Hb/g faeces (below threshold). Clinical picture is consistent with haemorrhoidal bleeding. Given his age, otherwise normal clinical examination, negative FIT, and absence of red flag features, two-week-wait referral is not indicated at this time. Advice given on dietary fibre, hydration, and avoidance of straining. Topical haemorrhoidal cream (lidocaine/hydrocortisone combination) prescribed. If bleeding persists beyond six weeks, recurs after resolution, or any new symptoms develop (change in bowel habit, weight loss, altered stool form), the patient is to return promptly for further assessment and FIT re-testing. Clear written safety net provided.

56F referred by optometrist for investigation of an incidentally noted choroidal lesion on routine fundal examination. She had attended for a new glasses prescription and has no ocular symptoms — no visual loss, no floaters, no photopsia. PMH: well-controlled hypothyroidism (levothyroxine 100mcg daily), no cutaneous melanoma history, no known malignancy, no family history of ocular melanoma. Vitals: BP 128/78, HR 70, afebrile. Ophthalmology review today: dilated fundoscopy and B-scan ultrasound confirm a pigmented choroidal lesion in the left eye, 2.1 x 1.9mm in basal diameter, 1.0mm in height — classified as small. No overlying subretinal fluid. No orange pigment identified. No symptoms. No documented growth at this stage — no prior baseline available for comparison. The lesion has several features associated with low risk (small size, no subretinal fluid, no symptoms) but absence of orange pigment and small size do not exclude early choroidal melanoma. Fundal photography and optical coherence tomography performed for baseline documentation. Liver USS arranged to screen for subclinical metastatic disease. Systemic haematology and oncology notified for awareness. Repeat ophthalmology review in three months for growth assessment. Patient counselled on the nature of the finding and instructed to report any new visual symptoms immediately. Levothyroxine continued unchanged.

Pt is a 67 y/o Black male with longstanding HTN x 22 years, poorly controlled on two agents, presenting today for routine follow-up with complaint of increasing exertional dyspnea over the past 6 weeks and bilateral ankle swelling. He reports no chest pain, no orthopnea, and no PND. Denies syncope. PMH significant for T2DM, CKD stage 3 (baseline Cr 1.8), and gout. Social history notable for 30-pack-year smoking history, quit 5 years ago. Current meds: amlodipine 10mg QD, lisinopril 20mg QD, metformin 1000mg BID, allopurinol 300mg QD.

On exam today, BP 162/98 mmHg (R arm), 160/96 mmHg (L arm), HR 88 bpm and regular, RR 16, O2 sat 96% on room air, weight 104 kg (up 4 kg from last visit 3 months ago). JVD present at 8 cm. Lungs with bibasilar crackles to mid-fields. 2+ pitting edema bilateral lower extremities to mid-shin. Cardiac exam notable for displaced PMI, S4 gallop, no murmurs appreciated.

ECG today shows LVH by voltage criteria with lateral ST depression. BNP returned at 540 pg/mL. BMP notable for Na 138, K 4.9, Cr 2.1 (up from 1.8), BUN 34, glucose 148. Echo ordered. CXR shows cardiomegaly with pulmonary vascular congestion and small bilateral pleural effusions.

Impression: Hypertensive heart disease with decompensated heart failure, likely HFpEF. CKD stage 3 with acute-on-chronic worsening, possibly related to cardiorenal syndrome.

Plan: Starting furosemide 40mg PO QD for diuresis, will recheck BMP and weight in 5 days by phone. Uptitrating lisinopril to 40mg is deferred given Cr bump. Adding carvedilol 3.125mg BID and will uptitrate. Metformin held given CKD worsening — messaging pt to hold until Cr reassessed. Echo scheduled for next week. Strict 2L fluid restriction and 2g Na diet reinforced. Return to clinic in 2 weeks or sooner if weight increases >2 lbs in a day or dyspnea worsens. Referral to nephrology placed.

39 y/o African American woman presenting with a 4-month history of progressive dyspnea on exertion, non-productive cough, and fatigue. She also endorses bilateral ankle pain and a skin rash on her shins that appeared around the same time. No fevers, no night sweats, no hemoptysis. She works as a schoolteacher, no known occupational exposures. Non-smoker. No significant PMH. No current medications. Family history unremarkable.

Vitals: Temp 37.1°C, HR 78, BP 118/74, RR 18, O2 sat 95% on room air, BMI 24. Exam reveals erythematous, tender, raised nodules on bilateral anterior shins consistent with erythema nodosum. Bilateral hilar fullness appreciated on auscultation is difficult to confirm clinically but CXR obtained today shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with a fine reticular pattern in the mid-lung zones, Scadding stage II. Pulmonary function testing shows a mild restrictive pattern: FVC 74% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.82. DLCO reduced at 68% predicted. CBC, CMP, and UA largely unremarkable. ACE level elevated at 92 U/L (normal <40). Serum calcium 10.8 mg/dL, urine calcium/creatinine ratio pending. 24-hr urine calcium ordered. LDH 280.

Bronchoscopy with BAL and transbronchial biopsy scheduled with pulmonology. Ophthalmology referral placed to evaluate for uveitis. Dermatology referral placed regarding erythema nodosum, though skin biopsy may be deferred if transbronchial biopsy confirms non-caseating granulomas. Given preserved respiratory function and erythema nodosum (which may indicate a self-limiting course, Löfgren-like syndrome), initiating steroids is deferred until tissue confirmation unless symptoms worsen.

Naproxen 500mg BID with food started for ankle pain and erythema nodosum, up to 2 weeks. Patient counseled extensively on sarcoidosis, its variable course, and the importance of follow-up. She was given written materials. Next visit in 3–4 weeks to review biopsy results. If biopsy confirms sarcoid and PFTs worsen, will initiate prednisone 20–40mg QD.

27 y/o white female referred by PCP for evaluation of fatigue, weight gain of approximately 8 lbs over 4 months, cold intolerance, constipation, and depressed mood. She initially attributed her symptoms to stress and a recent move, but PCP obtained thyroid labs that prompted this referral. She has no personal or family history of thyroid disease, though her mother has "some kind of autoimmune condition." Meds: none. No allergies. Non-smoker, drinks alcohol socially.

In clinic today: Temp 36.4°C, HR 58, BP 108/68, weight 72 kg. On exam she appears mildly fatigued. Skin is dry, hair is coarse and brittle. DTRs are delayed in the patellar reflex bilaterally. Thyroid is mildly enlarged, smooth, and non-tender with a firm rubbery texture. No lymphadenopathy. No periorbital edema. No signs of Graves' orbitopathy.

Labs from PCP: TSH 14.2 mIU/L, Free T4 0.7 ng/dL. TPO antibodies 480 IU/mL (ref <35). Anti-thyroglobulin antibodies 210 IU/mL. CBC and CMP within normal limits. Lipid panel: LDL 148 mg/dL, TG 195 mg/dL. Thyroid ultrasound obtained today shows a diffusely heterogeneous echotexture with coarsened parenchyma and increased vascularity, gland volume 22 mL — findings consistent with Hashimoto's thyroiditis. No discrete nodules identified.

Diagnosis: Hashimoto's thyroiditis with overt hypothyroidism. Started levothyroxine 75 mcg PO QAM on empty stomach. Discussed the importance of not taking calcium or iron supplements within 4 hours of dose. Lipid panel likely secondary to hypothyroid state and will recheck after euthyroid. Will recheck TSH and Free T4 in 6 weeks and titrate dose accordingly. Target TSH 1–2.5 mIU/L. Patient instructed that she will likely require lifelong thyroid replacement and that medication doses may need periodic adjustment, particularly if she becomes pregnant in the future (advised to contact office immediately if she conceives). Follow-up in 6 weeks.

33 y/o female with a 2-year history of relapsing-remitting MS diagnosed after an episode of left optic neuritis, presenting for a follow-up visit after a new relapse over the past 3 weeks. She describes right arm weakness, clumsiness in her right hand making it difficult to type, and a new sensation of electric shock-like pain radiating down her spine when she flexes her neck (Lhermitte's sign). She denies bowel or bladder involvement. She has been on interferon beta-1a (Avonex) 30 mcg IM weekly since diagnosis.

Vitals stable. EDSS estimated at 2.5 today (mild functional impairment). Neurological exam: right upper extremity pronator drift present, grip strength 4/5 on right vs 5/5 on left, finger-to-nose slightly dysmetric on right. Hyperreflexia right UE. Sensation intact. Vision 20/20 bilaterally, no relative afferent pupillary defect currently. Funduscopy normal.

MRI brain and cervical spine with and without gadolinium obtained this week. Brain shows 2 new T2 FLAIR lesions in the right periventricular region and one new lesion at C4 with gadolinium enhancement, indicating active inflammation. Overall lesion burden has increased compared to 18-month-old prior MRI.

Given clinical relapse with new enhancing lesion and evidence of disease activity on DMT, discussion initiated regarding escalation of therapy. Methylprednisolone 1g IV QD x3 days scheduled for this relapse to hasten recovery. Interferon beta-1a will be discontinued after completing pulse course. Referred back to MS neurology for formal discussion of high-efficacy DMT options including natalizumab, ocrelizumab, and alemtuzumab — given disease activity on first-line therapy, this conversation is timely. Baclofen 5mg BID added for spasticity as needed. PT/OT referral placed for right hand weakness. Patient is aware of the complexity of her situation and expressed understanding; she has questions about family planning which will be addressed at neurology visit given DMT implications.

Pt is a 24 y/o male, first established with this practice, referred from urgent care after two months of worsening crampy abdominal pain predominantly in the right lower quadrant, non-bloody diarrhea averaging 6 loose stools daily, a 10-lb unintentional weight loss, and subjective fevers. He was initially treated for presumed infectious gastroenteritis but stool cultures were negative. His older sister has Crohn's disease. He smokes about 0.5 PPD. No prior surgeries. No current medications.

Today: Temp 37.8°C, HR 94, BP 112/70, weight 61 kg (lost 4.5 kg in past month per records), BMI 19.4. Abdomen tender in RLQ with voluntary guarding, no rebound, no masses palpated. Perianal exam reveals a skin tag and a small non-draining perianal fissure. No fistulae visible.

Labs: CBC shows Hgb 10.4 g/dL, MCV 78, WBC 11.8, platelets 490 (thrombocytosis). CRP 48 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/hr. Albumin 2.8 g/dL. Fe 28, ferritin 8, TIBC 480 — iron deficiency anemia. B12 and folate normal. Fecal calprotectin >1000 mcg/g (markedly elevated). Stool C diff negative. ANA negative. CMP unremarkable.

CT enterography obtained today showing segmental transmural thickening of terminal ileum, approximately 22 cm in length, with mural stratification, surrounding fat stranding, and a few small mesenteric lymph nodes. No abscess or free perforation. Findings are highly suggestive of active Crohn's ileitis.

Formal GI referral expedited (appointment in 5 days). Upper and lower endoscopy with ileoscopy scheduled to confirm diagnosis, characterize extent, and obtain tissue. In the interim, starting budesonide 9mg QD x 8 weeks as bridge therapy given active symptoms; discussed with GI fellow. Iron supplementation: ferrous sulfate 325mg TID with orange juice. Smoking cessation counseled strongly — patient aware smoking worsens Crohn's disease course; NRT patch offered, declined today. Nutritional support discussed, ensure supplemental drink recommended. Education given on IBD, biologics (anticipate initiating anti-TNF therapy post-endoscopy), and monitoring. Return to clinic or GI in 1 week.

58 y/o female with a 6-month history of bilateral hand and wrist joint pain and stiffness, worse in the morning lasting greater than 2 hours, with associated fatigue and malaise. She initially dismissed symptoms as aging but presented after noting visible swelling and difficulty opening jars and buttoning clothing. Past history: controlled HTN, GERD. Current meds: amlodipine 5mg QD, omeprazole 20mg QD. Family history: mother with RA.

Vitals unremarkable. BMI 26. MSK exam: bilateral MCP (2nd–4th) and PIP joints warm, swollen, and tender to palpation. Wrists bilaterally with limited range of motion and synovial thickening. Grip strength reduced bilaterally. No rheumatoid nodules. No rashes. Lungs clear. No lymphadenopathy.

RF positive at 120 IU/mL. Anti-CCP antibody 280 U/mL (strongly positive). ANA positive 1:80 homogeneous, dsDNA negative, anti-Smith negative. CRP 22 mg/L, ESR 64 mm/hr. CBC: mild normocytic anemia, Hgb 11.2. CMP normal, LFTs normal. Hepatitis B sAg negative, HBsAb positive, HCV Ab negative (pre-biologic screening). Quantiferon-TB Gold negative. X-rays of hands and wrists show periarticular osteopenia at bilateral MCPs and early marginal erosion at the right 2nd MCP. No joint space narrowing yet.

Impression: Seropositive RA with early erosive disease. Rheumatology referral placed (appointment in 2 weeks); this note prepared for handoff. Initiating methotrexate 10mg PO weekly with folate 1mg QD (to be uptitrated to 15–25mg as tolerated under rheumatology guidance). Discussed teratogenicity and need for contraception. LFTs and CBC to be checked every 4–6 weeks during dose escalation. Hydroxychloroquine 400mg QD started concurrently as combination DMARD strategy — baseline ophthalmology exam ordered. Prednisone 10mg QD x 2 weeks as bridge while DMARDs take effect, then taper. Naproxen deferred given GERD history. Patient referred to occupational therapy for joint protection techniques. Follow-up with rheumatology in 2–3 weeks.

Disease: INFECTIOUS DISEASE — Complicated Urinary Tract Infection / Pyelonephritis
Note:
44 y/o female with PMH of recurrent UTIs and T2DM (A1c 9.1% last checked 4 months ago), presenting to urgent care with 3-day history of dysuria, urinary frequency, left flank pain, nausea, and fever to 38.9°C at home. She denies vaginal discharge. Last UTI was 5 months ago treated with nitrofurantoin. Current meds: metformin 500mg BID (inconsistently taken per patient).

Vitals: Temp 38.7°C, HR 104, BP 104/68, RR 18, O2 sat 98% RA. CVA tenderness marked on left side, mild on right. Abdomen soft, no peritoneal signs. No suprapubic tenderness. Normal skin turgor, mucous membranes slightly dry.

UA: cloudy, large leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, >50 WBCs/hpf, many bacteria. Urine culture sent — prior culture 5 months ago grew E. coli sensitive to nitrofurantoin, resistant to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. CBC: WBC 16.2 with 88% neutrophils, Hgb 12.1, platelets 320. BMP: Cr 1.1 (baseline unknown), glucose 218, BUN 22. Lactate 1.6. Blood cultures x2 sent prior to antibiotics given fever and signs of systemic infection.

Dx: Acute pyelonephritis in the setting of poorly controlled T2DM. Received 1L NS IV bolus in clinic. Given fever, tachycardia, and immunocompromised state, decision made to treat as potentially complicated: IV ceftriaxone 1g given as single IV dose in clinic. Prescribing ciprofloxacin 500mg PO BID x 7 days pending culture sensitivities — if culture shows resistance, will contact patient and amend. Metformin held while Cr uncertain. Push fluids at home, ORS advised. Return for blood culture follow-up in 48 hours (or ED if worsening fever, rigors, hypotension). Diabetes management to be addressed at follow-up — referral to endocrine placed. Instructions on hygiene reinforced. Repeat UA and urine culture at follow-up.

52 y/o male presenting for evaluation of a chronic skin condition that he has had intermittently for 15 years but has significantly worsened over the past 8 months. He describes thick, scaly plaques on his elbows, knees, scalp, and lower back that are pruritic and occasionally crack and bleed. He has used over-the-counter hydrocortisone and tar shampoos with minimal effect. He denies joint pain currently. PMH: obesity (BMI 38), metabolic syndrome, HTN. Meds: losartan 50mg QD, atorvastatin 20mg QD. Notable family history of psoriasis in father. He drinks 3–4 beers nightly.

Skin exam: well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery-white scale involving bilateral extensor elbows (largest ~6 x 4 cm), bilateral knees, posterior scalp (thick scale throughout), and lumbosacral region. Positive Auspitz sign. PASI score calculated at 18 (moderate-to-severe). Nails show onycholysis and pitting of bilateral thumbnails. No active arthritis or joint swelling appreciated today, though he notes occasional brief stiffness in his fingers upon waking — will monitor for psoriatic arthritis.

DLQI score 16 (very large effect on quality of life). Labs: CMP normal, CBC normal, fasting glucose 118, HbA1c 6.3%, lipids stable on statin. Hepatitis B/C and TB screening sent in anticipation of biologic therapy.

Given moderate-to-severe PASI and significant impact on QOL, topical therapy alone is insufficient. Dermatology referral placed. In the interim: clobetasol propionate 0.05% cream BID for body plaques (max 50g/week, no more than 4 consecutive weeks), fluocinonide solution 0.05% to scalp nightly under shower cap, and calcipotriene 0.005% ointment BID alternating with clobetasol to reduce steroid exposure. Discussed weight loss and alcohol reduction — evidence strongly suggests both worsen psoriasis and blunt treatment response. Referred to hepatology-adjacent screening for biologic candidacy (TNF inhibitor or IL-17/IL-23 inhibitor). Patient advised to keep skin moisturized with fragrance-free emollient. Follow-up with dermatology in 4–6 weeks.

29 y/o Asian male presenting with two episodes of gross hematuria, both occurring 1–2 days after URI symptoms (synpharyngitic hematuria), over the past 6 months. He describes the urine as dark/cola-colored lasting 1–2 days each time, resolving spontaneously. He has no dysuria, no flank pain, no recent travel, no family history of kidney disease. No current meds. Non-smoker. No occupational exposures.

BP today 136/88 mmHg (confirmed elevated, 134/90 on repeat, R arm seated) — notably elevated for his age. HR 72, BMI 23, no edema. No rash or purpura. No arthralgias. Funduscopy normal — no hypertensive retinopathy. No lymphadenopathy.

UA: 3+ blood, 1+ protein. Microscopy: dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts confirmed. Urine protein/creatinine ratio 0.82 (significant proteinuria). Serum Cr 1.1 mg/dL, eGFR ~82 mL/min/1.73m². Albumin 3.9 g/dL. Complement C3 and C4 normal. ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM, anti-streptolysin O all negative. Hepatitis B and C negative. IgA level 480 mg/dL (elevated, ref 70–400). IgG and IgM normal.

Renal ultrasound: kidneys normal size and echogenicity bilaterally, no hydronephrosis, no masses.

Clinical picture is highly suggestive of IgA nephropathy; differential includes thin basement membrane disease, though the clinical-synpharyngitic pattern, elevated IgA, and RBC casts make IgAN most likely. Nephrology referral placed — renal biopsy to be discussed with nephrology to confirm diagnosis and guide therapy. Starting lisinopril 5mg QD for blood pressure management and nephroprotective effect, targeting BP <125/75 and proteinuria reduction. Recheck BP, Cr, and UPCR in 4 weeks. High fish oil intake discussed (omega-3s), patient will consider. Low sodium diet counseled. Defer immunosuppression pending biopsy results. Discussed prognosis — variable but many patients do well with appropriate management. Pt to avoid NSAIDs and nephrotoxins. Follow-up in 4 weeks.

Disease: HEMATOLOGIC — Iron Deficiency Anemia (Premenopausal Woman, Cause Under Investigation)
Note:
38 y/o female presenting after PCP noted Hgb 8.2 g/dL on routine labs obtained for fatigue workup. She reports fatigue and exertional dyspnea over about 4 months, and on direct questioning endorses pica (craving and chewing ice, pagophagia). She has noted heavy menstrual periods for years but denies any change in cycle recently. She has no hematochezia, melena, hemoptysis, or hematuria. No weight loss. No prior anemia. No relevant family history. Meds: none. No prior surgeries.

Vitals: HR 100 (mildly elevated), BP 108/68, O2 sat 99%, BMI 22. Exam: conjunctival pallor bilaterally, mild pallor of palmar creases, mild tachycardia, heart sounds normal with a soft flow murmur at apex (grade II/VI). No lymphadenopathy. No hepatosplenomegaly. No petechiae or purpura.

CBC: Hgb 8.2 g/dL, MCV 68 fL, MCH 21 pg, RDW 18.5%. WBC and platelets normal. Retic count 0.8% (low, consistent with hypoproliferative pattern). Iron studies: serum Fe 22 mcg/dL, ferritin 4 ng/mL, TIBC 580 mcg/dL — classic iron deficiency. B12 normal, folate normal, hemoglobin electrophoresis normal (ruling out thalassemia). TSH normal. Peripheral smear: microcytic hypochromic RBCs, pencil cells present.

Plan: The degree of anemia and ferritin this low suggest both a source of blood loss and inadequate dietary intake. Menorrhagia is the most likely etiology, but GI blood loss needs to be excluded. GYN referral placed regarding heavy menstrual periods (consider hormonal management or fibroid workup). Stool guaiac tested today — result pending. If positive, colorectal GI referral will follow. Starting ferrous sulfate 325mg (65mg elemental iron) TID on empty stomach with vitamin C. Counseled on GI side effects (constipation, nausea) and dark stools. Dietary counseling on iron-rich foods. Recheck CBC and iron studies in 4 weeks. If GI blood loss suspected, upper and lower endoscopy to be arranged. Follow-up in 6 weeks.

Disease: PSYCHIATRIC — Major Depressive Disorder with Anxious Distress
Note:
46 y/o divorced male presenting at the request of his employee assistance program after a documented decline in work performance. Patient endorses a 5-month history of persistent depressed mood, anhedonia (no longer enjoys woodworking or watching sports), hypersomnia (sleeping 11–12 hours and still exhausted), weight gain of 14 lbs, psychomotor slowing, poor concentration, feelings of worthlessness, and passive death ideation ("I'd be fine if I didn't wake up") without suicidal plan or intent. He also describes near-constant worry and muscle tension. He denies manic episodes, psychotic symptoms, or prior psychiatric treatment. He drinks approximately 5–6 beers per weekend (denies daily use). FH: father with depression, suicide attempt at age 50. Patient is currently not in a relationship; limited social support — one close friend.

Vitals: unremarkable. PHQ-9 score 20 (severe depression). GAD-7 score 14 (moderate anxiety). Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale assessment completed: passive ideation, no plan/intent/history of attempts. TSH, CBC, CMP, B12, folate all within normal limits (ruling out reversible causes). Urine drug screen negative.

Diagnosis: Major depressive disorder, severe, with anxious distress. No suicidal plan but passive ideation acknowledged; safety plan developed and documented in chart — patient identified one friend to call, agreed to present to ED if ideation becomes active. Starting sertraline 50mg QD, with plan to increase to 100mg in 2 weeks if tolerated. Discussed SSRI lag time of 4–6 weeks. Counseled against alcohol use — interaction with mood and sleep addressed. Referring to individual CBT-based psychotherapy; intake scheduled. Sleep hygiene education provided. Return in 2 weeks to reassess tolerability, PHQ-9, and safety. If no improvement in 6 weeks on adequate dose, will consider augmentation or psychiatry referral. Patient given crisis line number (988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline). Importance of follow-up appointment emphasized.

67 y/o hyperopic female presenting to urgent care with a 4-hour history of sudden onset severe right eye pain, blurred vision, colored halos around lights, frontal headache, nausea, and one episode of vomiting. Denies prior eye surgery, recent trauma, or prior similar episodes. PMH: HTN, hyperopia (wears reading glasses). Meds: hydrochlorothiazide 25mg QD. No current eye drops.

Vitals: BP 178/98 (elevated, likely pain-related), HR 88. Right eye: pupil mid-dilated (~6mm) and poorly reactive to light. Cornea appears hazy/steamy on penlight exam. Eye is injected (diffuse conjunctival injection). Marked tenderness with gentle palpation of globe — firm compared to left eye. Visual acuity right eye: 20/200; left eye: 20/25 with correction. Left eye exam normal.

Tonometry (Schiotz): right IOP ~48 mmHg, left IOP 14 mmHg (urgent concern). Gonioscopy and formal slit lamp exam by ophthalmology is needed.

Ophthalmology emergency paged — patient being transferred directly. While awaiting transport: Timolol 0.5% 1 drop right eye, brimonidine 0.1% 1 drop right eye, and acetazolamide 500mg PO given to reduce IOP acutely. Patient positioned supine. Pilocarpine 2% 1 drop instilled to constrict pupil and open angle. IV ondansetron 4mg given for nausea. Patient and family informed that this is an ophthalmologic emergency and that permanent vision loss can occur without immediate treatment. Laser peripheral iridotomy is likely to be performed by ophthalmology today. Left eye may be prophylactically treated as well given bilateral anatomical risk in hyperopic patients. Patient instructed not to take any anticholinergic medications in the future without ophthalmology clearance.

Disease: RHEUMATOLOGIC — Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (New Presentation Under Workup)
Note:
22 y/o female of Afro-Caribbean descent presenting with a 3-month history of intermittent facial rash worsened by sun exposure, bilateral symmetric hand and wrist joint pain and swelling, oral ulcers (noticed 3–4 times), patchy hair loss, extreme fatigue, and a recent episode of pleuritic chest pain that resolved spontaneously over 3 days. She denies seizures, psychosis, or significant headaches. No current medications. Non-smoker. Oral contraceptive pill use in the past; currently not on hormones. FH: aunt with lupus.

Vitals: Temp 37.5°C, HR 86, BP 116/72, BMI 21. Exam: malar rash present — butterfly distribution across cheeks and nasal bridge sparing nasolabial folds, non-scarring alopecia at temporal hairline, two small aphthous ulcers on buccal mucosa. MSK: swelling and tenderness at bilateral wrists and 2nd–4th MCPs, no deformity. Lungs clear today. No lymphadenopathy. No peripheral edema.

ANA positive 1:320 homogeneous pattern. Anti-dsDNA 142 IU/mL (significantly elevated, highly specific for SLE). Anti-Smith antibody positive. Complement C3 16 mg/dL (low), C4 4 mg/dL (low). CBC: WBC 3.1 (leukopenia), Hgb 10.6 (normocytic), platelets 140. Direct Coombs test positive. Urinalysis: 2+ protein, RBC 5–10/hpf, WBC 3–5/hpf. Urine protein/creatinine ratio 1.2 — concerning for lupus nephritis. Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, eGFR normal. CRP mildly elevated; ESR 72 mm/hr. Antiphospholipid panel sent (anti-cardiolipin, beta-2 glycoprotein I antibodies). CXR clear.

This presentation meets ≥4 SLE classification criteria and is clinically consistent with SLE, likely with early renal involvement. Rheumatology and nephrology referrals placed urgently. Renal biopsy likely to be recommended by nephrology to characterize nephritis class and guide immunosuppression intensity. Starting hydroxychloroquine 400mg QD (weight-based). Naproxen for joint pain and pleurisy as needed. High SPF sun protection and UV-protective clothing strongly advised. Folic acid supplementation. Will discuss oral contraception discontinuation with patient (estrogen-containing OCPs may exacerbate SLE). Patient counseled that this is a complex, manageable condition. Baseline ophthalmology exam for hydroxychloroquine monitoring scheduled. Follow-up with rheumatology in 1 week.

Pt is a 55 y/o female presenting with an 8-month history of progressive fatigue, unintentional weight loss of approximately 11 lbs, nausea, intermittent abdominal pain, salt craving, and dizziness on standing. She notes darkening of her skin — most notable on her knuckles, palmar creases, and gingiva — which her friends have commented on. She has a history of vitiligo and autoimmune thyroid disease (on levothyroxine 88 mcg QD). No other meds. No prior surgeries. FH: sister with T1DM.

Vitals: lying BP 110/68, standing BP 88/54 (orthostatic hypotension), HR 102 standing (orthostatic tachycardia). Temp 36.8°C, BMI 19 (down from 21.5 per old records). Notable hyperpigmentation of knuckles, gingiva, buccal mucosa, and palmar creases. Patchy vitiligo on bilateral forearms.

Labs: Na 128, K 5.8 (hyponatremia and hyperkalemia highly suggestive of mineralocorticoid deficiency). Cr 1.2, glucose 62. Cortisol AM (8 AM) 3.4 mcg/dL (severely low, normal >18 in our lab). ACTH stimulation test performed: baseline cortisol 3.2, 30-min post-cosyntropin 5.8 mcg/dL — suboptimal response, confirming adrenal insufficiency. ACTH level markedly elevated at 1,820 pg/mL (normal <46) — confirms primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease). 21-hydroxylase antibodies positive — autoimmune etiology confirmed. DHEA-S undetectable. Aldosterone 2 ng/dL (low), plasma renin activity elevated. CXR and abdominal CT obtained to rule out adrenal TB/infiltrative process — adrenal glands appear small bilaterally, consistent with autoimmune atrophy. No active TB.

Initiated hydrocortisone 15mg PO QAM and 5mg at 2 PM (to mimic diurnal cortisol pattern). Starting fludrocortisone 0.1mg QAM for mineralocorticoid replacement. Patient prescribed emergency hydrocortisone injection kit (Solu-Cortef 100mg IM) and given extensive written and verbal education on sick day rules — dose doubling for fevers/minor illness, triple dosing for major stress, and when to administer IM injection (vomiting, unable to take oral medications, altered consciousness). Medical alert bracelet strongly recommended and ordered. Endocrinology follow-up in 4 weeks. Electrolytes and BP to be checked at 2 weeks. Patient's levothyroxine dose held constant for now — cortisol replacement may alter thyroid requirements, recheck TSH at 6 weeks.

21 y/o male college student presenting after his second episode of sudden-onset palpitations with near-syncope over the past 3 months. Each episode begins abruptly, lasts approximately 20–30 minutes, and terminates suddenly. He describes a racing "flutter" in his chest at rates he estimates as "extremely fast." He denies chest pain or frank syncope, though notes lightheadedness. His first episode was in the gym; today's was while sitting watching TV. He drinks caffeine (3–4 energy drinks daily). No known cardiac history. FH: maternal uncle with SVT, no sudden cardiac death. No meds, no supplements. Non-smoker.

Vitals at rest today: HR 78 and regular, BP 118/72, O2 sat 100%. Cardiac exam normal — regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, no S3/S4. No signs of heart failure. Normal JVP.

12-lead ECG during sinus rhythm: normal sinus rhythm, no delta waves (ruling out WPW), QTc 408 ms, no LVH or prior infarct changes. Echo ordered today — returned normal cardiac structure and function, EF 65%, no structural defect. TSH normal. CBC and BMP normal. Electrolytes normal. Troponin not indicated.

Given episodic nature, age, and clinical pattern, paroxysmal SVT (AVNRT most likely) is the leading diagnosis. Ambulatory cardiac monitoring (14-day event monitor) ordered to capture future episode and characterize rhythm. Counseled on vagal maneuvers — modified Valsalva technique demonstrated and printed instructions given. Caffeine and energy drink reduction strongly advised as a modifiable trigger — patient agreed to cut down. Metoprolol succinate 25mg QD offered as prophylactic rate control — patient prefers to try caffeine reduction first, to be reassessed. If event monitor confirms AVNRT and episodes remain frequent or symptomatic, will discuss electrophysiology referral for catheter ablation (curative in >95% of cases). Return in 4 weeks or sooner if prolonged or poorly tolerated episode occurs; if hemodynamic instability occurs, instructed to call 911.

51 y/o Hispanic male presenting for follow-up of abnormal LFTs identified incidentally during a life insurance screening. He has been asymptomatic but does endorse fatigue and some right upper quadrant discomfort described as "heaviness." PMH: T2DM (A1c 8.4%), hypertriglyceridemia, hypertension, obesity (BMI 36). Meds: metformin 1000mg BID, lisinopril 10mg QD, fenofibrate 145mg QD. Alcohol: 1–2 beers weekly. Non-smoker.

Vitals: BP 138/88, HR 76, weight 112 kg. Abdomen notable for central obesity. Liver edge palpable 3 cm below right costal margin; mild tenderness with deep palpation. No stigmata of chronic liver disease (no spider angiomata, no palmar erythema, no caput medusae, no asterixis). No splenomegaly appreciated.

LFTs: ALT 78 U/L, AST 62 U/L (AST/ALT <1), total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, ALP 92 U/L, albumin 4.0 g/dL, total protein 7.2 g/dL, INR 1.0. Repeat LFTs today confirm persistent elevation x 3 months now. Triglycerides 380 mg/dL. ANA negative, anti-smooth muscle antibody negative (excluding autoimmune hepatitis). Ceruloplasmin and alpha-1 antitrypsin normal. Hepatitis A IgG positive (immune), HBsAg negative, HBsAb positive, HCV Ab negative. Ferritin 620 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 28% — elevated ferritin likely inflammatory.

Liver ultrasound: markedly increased hepatic echogenicity with posterior attenuation consistent with hepatic steatosis, grade 3. Liver span 18 cm. FIB-4 index calculated: 1.9 (intermediate — hepatology referral appropriate). Vibration-controlled transient elastography (FibroScan) ordered. Hepatology referral placed to consider liver biopsy given elevated FIB-4, degree of steatosis, and metabolic risk factors — need to assess for significant fibrosis.

Counseled extensively on weight loss — a 7–10% body weight reduction can significantly improve NASH histology. Structured diet referral (Mediterranean diet) and exercise prescription given. Optimizing diabetes management — will transition to semaglutide 0.5mg SQ weekly (evidence for improvement in NASH and concurrent benefit for T2DM and weight loss); metformin continued. Vitamin E 800 IU QD considered, deferred until biopsy confirms NASH without cirrhosis, as is standard. Alcohol cessation (even low amounts) recommended. Follow-up in 3 months with repeat LFTs and FIB-4.

34 y/o female presenting with a 7-month history of recurrent episodes of wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath primarily triggered by exercise, cold air, and occasionally workplace perfumes. She also wakes from sleep with cough and wheeze about 2 nights per week. She has been using an albuterol inhaler borrowed from her roommate approximately 4–5 times per week. She was treated for "bronchitis" twice in the past year with azithromycin and short prednisone courses with transient improvement. PMH: allergic rhinitis, childhood eczema (resolved). FH: mother with asthma. Meds: loratadine 10mg PRN. Works in a salon — chemical and fragrance exposure daily.

Vitals: SpO2 98% RA, RR 16, HR 74, BP 112/70. Chest: diffuse end-expiratory wheeze on forced expiration, otherwise clear. No accessory muscle use at rest. No nasal polyps. Mild nasal turbinate hypertrophy.

Spirometry today: FEV1 78% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.72 (obstructive pattern). Post-bronchodilator (400 mcg albuterol) FEV1 increases to 94% predicted (+16% and +280mL) — significant reversibility confirming bronchial asthma. FeNO 42 ppb (elevated, consistent with eosinophilic airway inflammation and predicting ICS responsiveness). CBC: eosinophils 6%. IgE elevated at 280 IU/mL. Chest X-ray: no infiltrate, no pneumothorax, hyperinflation noted.

Diagnosis: Persistent moderate adult-onset asthma, likely allergic/eosinophilic phenotype. ACQ-6 score 2.1 (not well controlled). Initiating fluticasone/salmeterol (Advair) 250/50 one puff BID. Prescribing albuterol MDI 2 puffs PRN (patient's own supply). Inhaler technique demonstrated in clinic — spacer provided. Montelukast 10mg QD added given concurrent allergic rhinitis. Allergen skin testing referral placed to identify specific triggers. Occupational exposure discussed — patient will discuss with employer about improved ventilation and fragrance-free policy. Written asthma action plan provided. Patient instructed to contact clinic if using rescue inhaler >2x/week. Follow-up spirometry in 6–8 weeks to assess ICS response. ACQ will be repeated at next visit.

Disease: NEUROLOGICAL (Undiagnosed) — New Onset Headache with Focal Features
Note:
48 y/o male presenting for evaluation of a new headache pattern developing over the past 6 weeks. He describes a left-sided throbbing headache associated with left eye visual flickering and left hand paresthesias (numbness and tingling) that precede the headache by 20–30 minutes and resolve before the headache peaks. The headache lasts 4–8 hours, is moderately severe, worsened by light and noise, and accompanied by nausea. He has no prior headache history. He denies fever, nuchal rigidity, papilledema symptoms, or headache on awakening. No change in personality or memory. He notes headaches begin typically in the late afternoon. He works as a financial analyst, reports high stress. PMH: HTN on hydrochlorothiazide 25mg QD. Smokes 0.5 PPD for 20 years. Family history of migraine in maternal side.

Vitals: BP 148/92, HR 76. Full neurological exam performed: cranial nerves II–XII intact, no focal motor or sensory deficits between episodes (exam performed today when headache-free), no cerebellar signs, no papilledema on funduscopic exam, Romberg negative. MMSE 30/30.

Given new headache onset after age 45, focal neurological symptoms (visual, sensory), and HTN, the clinical concern for secondary headache (e.g., TIA, structural lesion, vascular malformation) alongside migraine with aura requires neuroimaging before confident labeling as primary headache. MRI brain with and without gadolinium and MRA head/neck ordered today. EEG ordered given sensory and visual phenomena. Neurology referral placed.

Empirically, the clinical features of unilateral throbbing headache + aura symptoms + nausea/photophobia are consistent with migraine with aura, but this cannot be assumed without ruling out secondary causes. Patient instructed to present to ED if any headache described as "worst of my life," associated with fever/stiff neck, new neurological deficit, or visual loss that does not resolve. Prescribing sumatriptan 50mg PO at onset of headache (with a second dose after 2 hours if headache returns, max 200mg/24h) as acute therapy pending neurology review. NSAIDs (naproxen 500mg) as alternative for milder headaches. Patient counseled on caffeine use, irregular sleep, and stress as potential triggers. No prophylactic therapy initiated until neuroimaging reviewed. Headache diary given. Follow-up once imaging obtained (within 1 week).

Disease: MUSCULOSKELETAL — Lumbar Disc Herniation with Radiculopathy
Note:
42 y/o male warehouse worker presenting with a 3-week history of low back pain radiating down the left leg in a classic L5 distribution — posterior thigh, lateral calf, and dorsum of the foot — onset after lifting a heavy pallet at work. Pain is 7/10 at rest, 9/10 with bending or prolonged sitting. He denies bowel or bladder dysfunction. No saddle anesthesia. PMH: obesity (BMI 34), ex-smoker. Current meds: ibuprofen 400mg PRN (minimally effective).

Vitals unremarkable. Exam: antalgic gait favoring right leg. Lumbar ROM severely limited — forward flexion 30°. SLR positive on left at 40°, negative on right. Crossed SLR negative. Neurological: left ankle dorsiflexion strength 4/5 (great toe extension mildly weak), sensation decreased to light touch on dorsum of left foot and first webspace. Achilles and patellar reflexes intact and symmetric. No myelopathic signs. No tenderness over spinous processes.

MRI lumbar spine (ordered by urgent care 1 week ago, results reviewed today): large left paracentral disc herniation at L4-L5 with extrusion, caudal migration, and significant compression of the left L5 nerve root in the lateral recess. Moderate disc height loss at L4-5. No central canal stenosis. L5-S1 disc mild bulge, clinically less relevant. No evidence of cauda equina involvement.

Impression: L4-L5 disc herniation with left L5 radiculopathy. No cauda equina syndrome. Presenting for conservative management at this time. Prescribing cyclobenzaprine 5mg QHS PRN for spasm (cautioned not to drive). Starting naproxen 500mg BID with food (DC ibuprofen), adding omeprazole 20mg QD for GI protection. A single course of oral methylprednisolone dose pack prescribed to reduce radicular inflammation. Referral for physical therapy (McKenzie approach, nerve mobilization). Discussed that most herniations improve with conservative management over 6–12 weeks. Return to work modified duty discussed and work note provided. If no improvement in 6 weeks, or if weakness worsens or bowel/bladder symptoms develop, urgent neurosurgery referral will be placed. Pain management referral placed for potential lumbar ESI if conservative therapy fails. STRICT instruction: if saddle anesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence develops — present to ED immediately.

Disease: AUTOIMMUNE — Myasthenia Gravis (New Onset Under Evaluation)
Note:
63 y/o female presenting with a 2-month history of progressive ptosis of the right eyelid (worse by late afternoon), intermittent binocular diplopia, and fatigue that she describes as worsening throughout the day — "I'm fine in the morning but by evening I can barely hold my eyelids open." She also reports mild difficulty chewing tough foods and occasional nasal voice quality. Denies dysphagia to liquids, limb weakness, or respiratory symptoms. PMH: autoimmune thyroid disease (on levothyroxine), well-controlled. FH: no neuromuscular disease. Meds: levothyroxine 75 mcg QD.

Vitals stable. BMI 24. Neurological exam: right ptosis noted (worsens with sustained upgaze at 30 seconds — fatigable). Ice pack test: ptosis notably improves after 2-minute ice pack application to right eye (positive test). Extraocular movements restricted with diplopia on right lateral gaze. Oropharyngeal exam: slight dysarthria with counting to 50 (voice fatigues). Neck flexor strength 4/5. No limb atrophy or fasiculations. No facial muscle weakness. Deep tendon reflexes intact. Spirometry requested — FVC 92% predicted (no respiratory compromise currently).

AChR binding antibodies: strongly positive at 8.2 nmol/L (highly specific for myasthenia gravis). Anti-MuSK antibody not required given AChR positive result. TSH checked — within normal range. CT chest with contrast: anterior mediastinal mass, ~3.5 cm, consistent with thymoma. No hilar adenopathy. No metastatic disease evident.

Neurology and thoracic surgery referrals placed urgently given thymoma. Thymectomy will be discussed and is likely indicated. Starting pyridostigmine (Mestinon) 30mg PO TID with meals initially, to be titrated for symptom control. No steroids initiated until neurology consultation — immunosuppression has particular considerations with thymoma. Patient and family counseled on myasthenic crisis — instructed not to take aminoglycosides, ciprofloxacin, magnesium, or other potentially contraindicated medications without physician clearance (list provided in writing). Instructed to go to ED if respiratory distress, severe dysphagia to liquids, or marked weakness occurs. Follow-up with neurology within 1 week.

Disease: Lung Cancer vs. Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
Note: Pt is a 64yo male with 40-pack-year smoking hx, quit 5 years ago, presenting with 3-month hx of worsening cough and mild dyspnea on exertion. He attributes this to a "smoker’s lingering cough" but notes a 5lb weight loss he thinks is from yard work. O2 sat 94% on RA, HR 88, afebrile. Lung sounds show faint wheezing in the right upper lobe that does not clear with cough. CXR shows some hyperinflation and a faint, ill-defined opacity in the RUL, possibly atelectasis or post-inflammatory scarring. Started on Salmeterol/Fluticasone inhaler twice daily. Scheduled for repeat CXR in 6 weeks and a pulmonary function test.

32yo female presents with persistent dry cough, night sweats, and "bumps" on her shins. She is extremely fatigued. Vital signs: BP 115/70, HR 92, Temp 100.1F. Physical exam reveals tender, erythematous nodules on bilateral pretibial surfaces and palpable, non-tender bilateral hilar adenopathy suggested by dullness on percussion, though heart sounds are normal. CBC shows mild leukopenia; ACE level is elevated at 95 U/L. Prescribed Naproxen 500mg BID for leg pain. Referral to Pulmonology for bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy to differentiate granulomatous disease from malignancy.

61yo male reports vague epigastric discomfort radiating to the mid-back, worse after heavy meals, for the last 8 weeks. No jaundice noted; sclera are clear. Weight is stable, though appetite is slightly diminished. He has a hx of GERD. Abdomen is soft, non-tender, no masses. Lipase is normal, LFTs show a trace elevation in alkaline phosphatase at 135 U/L, but Bilirubin is 0.8. Prescribed Omeprazole 40mg daily and told to avoid fatty foods. Follow-up in 4 weeks; if symptoms persist, will consider abdominal CT.

55yo female with intermittent left lower quadrant cramping and a recent change in bowel habits, alternating between constipation and thin stools. She has noticed occasional streaks of bright red blood, which she attributes to known internal hemorrhoids. BP 140/85, HR 78, Temp 99.0. Abdomen is mildly tender in the LLQ without rebound. Hemoglobin is 11.2, slightly down from her baseline of 13.0 last year. Prescribed a high-fiber diet and Ciprofloxacin/Metronidazole for presumed mild diverticulitis. Refers to GI for a colonoscopy once acute inflammation subsides.

45yo male, recent immigrant from an endemic region, presenting with hemoptysis, chronic cough, and drenching night sweats. He has lost 10lbs in 2 months. HR 105, Temp 101.2. Auscultation reveals rales in the left apex. Imaging shows a 3cm cavitary lesion in the left upper lobe with surrounding infiltrate. Sputum acid-fast bacilli stains are pending. Started on empiric RIPE therapy (Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol) pending culture results. Patient placed in respiratory isolation; Oncology consult deferred until TB status confirmed.

Disease: Early Ovarian Cancer vs. Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Note: 48yo female complains of increased abdominal bloating, pelvic "fullness," and urinary frequency over the past 4 months. She has tried OTC probiotics and fiber with no relief. Pelvic exam is difficult due to patient discomfort; no obvious adnexal masses palpated, but there is general fullness in the cul-de-sac. CA-125 is 42 U/mL (borderline). Prescribed Dicyclomine 10mg TID for suspected IBS-related spasms. Ordered a transvaginal ultrasound to be completed within the week.

39yo female presents with a "full feeling" in her neck and recent onset of palpitations and heat intolerance. She is anxious and has a fine tremor. HR 112, BP 150/90. On palpation, there is a firm, 2cm solitary nodule on the right lobe of the thyroid that moves with swallowing. TSH is suppressed at 0.05 mIU/L, Free T4 is elevated. Started on Methimazole 10mg daily and Propranolol 20mg BID. Scheduled for a radioactive iodine uptake scan and fine-needle aspiration to rule out a toxic nodule vs. occult malignancy.

Disease: Multiple Myeloma vs. Degenerative Disc Disease
Note: 70yo male with chronic lower back pain that has become "boring" and constant over the last month, now waking him at night. He denies any recent trauma. Physical exam shows localized tenderness over the L3-L4 vertebrae. No focal neurological deficits. ESR is 85 mm/hr, and Cr is slightly elevated at 1.4. X-ray shows osteopenia and some "punched out" lucencies that the radiologist suggests may be vascular markings but recommends clinical correlation. Prescribed Gabapentin 300mg at bedtime and scheduled for serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP).

Disease: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia vs. Prostate Cancer
Note: 68yo male with increasing urinary hesitancy, nocturia x4, and a weak stream. He reports one episode of gross hematuria after vigorous exercise. Digital rectal exam reveals a globally enlarged, firm prostate; a specific nodule is difficult to appreciate due to overall size. PSA is 6.5 ng/mL. Prescribed Tamsulosin 0.4mg daily. Patient to maintain a voiding diary and return for a repeat PSA and possible transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy if symptoms do not improve.

29yo female with severe pelvic pain that is non-cyclical and worsening. She reports deep dyspareunia and occasional spotting between periods. Abdomen is soft, but there is significant tenderness upon deep palpation of the left adnexa. Ultrasound shows a complex 5cm cystic mass on the left ovary with internal echoes, possibly an endometrioma. Prescribed continuous oral contraceptives to suppress menses and Ibuprofen 600mg as needed. Follow-up ultrasound in 8 weeks to monitor for size changes or internal solid components.

58yo male with a history of H. pylori infection presents with gnawing epigastric pain that is partially relieved by antacids but accompanied by early satiety. He has lost 8lbs involuntarily. Physical exam is unremarkable except for mild epigastric tenderness. Fecal occult blood test is positive. Prescribed a 14-day course of Clarithromycin, Amoxicillin, and Lansoprazole. Scheduled for an EGD (Esophagogastroduodenoscopy) to visualize the mucosa and biopsy any non-healing ulcerations.

Disease: Giant Cell Arteritis vs. Metastatic Skull Lesion
Note: 74yo female presents with new-onset left-sided headaches and "tenderness" when brushing her hair. She also reports some jaw claudication while chewing. BP 155/95, Temp 99.4. The left temporal artery is prominent and slightly tender to touch. ESR is 90 mm/hr. Concerned about vision loss, I have started her on Prednisone 60mg daily. Scheduled for a temporal artery biopsy. However, given her history of treated breast cancer 10 years ago, a PET/CT is also being considered if the biopsy is negative.

Disease: Inflammatory Bowel Disease vs. Lymphoma of the Bowel
Note: 22yo male presents with 6 months of bloody diarrhea, cramping, and a 15lb weight loss. He has frequent low-grade fevers. Abdominal exam reveals a palpable fullness in the RLQ. Hemoglobin 10.5, WBC 12.0. CT scan shows marked thickening of the terminal ileum and cecum with associated mesenteric lymphadenopathy. Prescribed Mesalamine and a short course of Prednisone for presumed Crohn’s disease. Referral to GI for colonoscopy with multiple biopsies to rule out atypical lymphoproliferative disorders.

Disease: Renal Calculi vs. Renal Cell Carcinoma
Note: 52yo male presents with intermittent right flank pain and microscopic hematuria found on a routine physical. He denies dysuria or fever. BP 152/94. A bedside ultrasound shows mild hydronephrosis on the right and a 3.5cm solid-appearing mass on the lower pole of the right kidney, which could be a complex cyst or a tumor. Prescribed Hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension and Flomax in case a small stone is passing. Ordered a dedicated renal mass CT protocol for further characterization.

Disease: Actinic Keratosis vs. Squamous Cell Carcinoma
Note: 65yo fair-skinned female with a "scaly patch" on her left temple that bleeds occasionally when she rubs it. It has been present for about a year. On exam, there is a 1.2cm erythematous, hyperkeratotic plaque with some induration at the base. No cervical lymphadenopathy. I have applied liquid nitrogen cryotherapy to the lesion today. Prescribed Fluorouracil 5% cream to be applied twice daily for two weeks. If the lesion does not resolve or if it recurs, a punch biopsy will be required.

Disease: Iron Deficiency Anemia vs. Occult GI Malignancy
Note: 72yo female feeling increasingly "washed out" and short of breath when climbing stairs. She denies any melena or hematochezia. HR 95, conjunctival pallor noted. Labs show Hgb 8.2, MCV 72, Ferritin 8. She has a history of daily aspirin use for cardioprotection. Prescribed Ferrous Sulfate 325mg daily. While the anemia may be secondary to ASA-induced erosive gastritis, given her age, she is scheduled for a dual workup with both colonoscopy and EGD.

Disease: Fibrocystic Breast Changes vs. Breast Cancer
Note: 42yo female notes a new "lump" in her left breast that she found during a shower. She says it feels somewhat tender and she thinks it gets larger before her period. On exam, there is a 2cm, somewhat mobile, rubbery mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. No skin dimpling or nipple discharge. Prescribed a reduction in caffeine intake and supportive bras. Ordered a diagnostic mammogram and targeted ultrasound to differentiate a simple cyst from a solid lesion.

50yo male of Cantonese descent presents with unilateral right-sided nasal congestion and occasional epistaxis for 4 months. He also mentions a "plugged" feeling in his right ear. He has been treated with two courses of Amoxicillin with minimal relief. Exam shows serous otitis media on the right. Prescribed Fluticasone nasal spray and Augmentin. Due to the unilateral nature of symptoms, I have placed an urgent referral to ENT for nasopharyngoscopy to visualize the fossa of Rosenmüller.

34yo lactating female (4 months postpartum) presents with a red, warm, and swollen right breast. She has a fever of 101.5. She has been self-treating with warm compresses with no improvement. Exam shows diffuse erythema over the lower half of the breast with some "orange peel" skin texture (peau d'orange) noted near the areola. No discrete abscess felt. Prescribed Dicloxacillin 500mg QID. I have instructed her to return in 72 hours; if there is no significant improvement in the skin changes, a skin punch biopsy will be necessary to rule out inflammatory malignancy.

55yo male with a 2-year history of "eczema" on his trunk and buttocks that hasn't responded well to OTC hydrocortisone. The patches are mildly itchy and look like thin, wrinkled red plates. Exam shows well-demarcated, dusky red, scaly plaques in "bathing suit" distribution. Prescribed Triamcinolone 0.1% ointment. Because the distribution is atypical for plaque psoriasis and the lesions are persistent, I have referred him to Dermatology for a biopsy to rule out cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.

Pt returns for f/u on stage IV NSCLC (adenocarcinoma). 64yo male, 40-pack-year smoker, currently undergoing 2nd line immunotherapy. Reports increased dyspnea on exertion and a persistent dry cough that keeps him up at night. O2 sat 92% on RA, HR 88, BP 132/84. Diminished breath sounds at the right base. CXR shows stable primary mass but new trace pleural effusion. Discussed palliative intent of current regimen. Continue pembrolizumab 200mg IV every 3 weeks. Start benzonatate 100mg TID PRN for cough. Scheduled for repeat CT chest/abdomen/pelvis in 4 weeks to assess treatment response.

72yo female presents with 15lb unintentional weight loss over 3 months and early satiety. History of chronic H. pylori infection treated 10 years ago. Physical exam reveals vague epigastric tenderness but no palpable masses. BP 110/70, Temp 98.4F. Lab work shows microcytic anemia with Hgb 9.2 g/dL. Occult blood positive in stool. Suspect gastric CA vs. peptic ulcer disease. Rx: Pantoprazole 40mg QD. Referral placed for urgent EGD/colonoscopy. Pt to keep food diary and report any melena or hematemesis immediately.

Post-op day 14 f/u for 55yo male with WHO Grade 4 Glioblastoma. Spouse reports patient has been more somnolent with occasional expressive aphasia. Incision is healing well, no signs of infection. Vitals stable. MRI brain shows expected post-surgical changes with significant peri-tumoral edema. We will begin the Stupp protocol. Prescription for Temozolomide 75 mg/m² daily during RT. Increase Dexamethasone to 4mg BID to manage cerebral edema. Start Levetiracetam 500mg BID for seizure prophylaxis. F/u with Radiation Oncology tomorrow for mask fitting.

48yo female with Stage IIA (T2N0M0) ER+/PR+/HER2- IDC of the left breast. Pt is 3 days post-lumpectomy and sentinel lymph node biopsy. Pain is well-controlled with ibuprofen. No fever or redness at the site. BP 124/78, HR 72. Path report confirms clear margins; sentinel nodes negative. We discussed the transition to adjuvant therapy. Rx: Tamoxifen 20mg daily for 5 years. Refer to Medical Oncology for discussion of Oncotype DX testing to determine benefit of chemotherapy. F/u in clinic in 2 weeks for wound check.

22yo male presents with a "lump" in the left supraclavicular region, first noted 3 weeks ago. Pt also reports drenching night sweats and intermittent low-grade fevers (100.2F). No recent viral illnesses or travel. On exam, a 2.5cm rubbery, non-tender, fixed lymph node is noted in the Left Virchow’s space. CBC shows mild lymphocytosis. LDH is elevated at 280 U/L. CT neck/chest ordered today. Rx: Ibuprofen 400mg PRN for discomfort. Scheduled for excisional biopsy of the node on Friday. Pt educated on B-symptoms and when to call the on-call service.

61yo male with known borderline resectable pancreatic head mass. Pt presents today with worsening jaundice and pruritus. Scleral icterus noted. BP 130/82, HR 94. Total bilirubin elevated at 8.4 mg/dL; CA 19-9 is 1,200 U/mL. Abdominal CT shows biliary ductal dilation. Surgery scheduled for ERCP with stent placement to relieve biliary obstruction before initiating neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX. Rx: Creon 24,000 units with meals; Oxycodone 5mg q6h PRN for abdominal pain. Return to clinic post-stenting to coordinate chemo start date.

59yo male with incidental finding of a 4cm solid mass on the left kidney during workup for nephrolithiasis. Pt is asymptomatic, no hematuria. BP 145/90, otherwise vitals normal. Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL. CT abdomen/pelvis confirms a Bosniak IV lesion. Discussed options including partial vs. total nephrectomy. Pt prefers organ-sparing approach if feasible. Rx: Amlodipine 5mg daily to optimize BP prior to surgery. Scheduled for robotic-assisted partial nephrectomy next Tuesday.

34yo female admitted for induction chemotherapy following bone marrow biopsy confirming AML (FLT3 positive). Pt is currently neutropenic with ANC of 200. Temp 101.5F, HR 110. Started on broad-spectrum antibiotics (Cefepime) per neutropenic fever protocol. Cultures pending. Hgb 7.4, Plt 18k; transfusing 1 unit PRBCs and 1 unit platelets today. Continue 7+3 regimen (Cytarabine/Idarubicin) with addition of Midostaurin. Monitor vitals Q4H. Daily CBC and electrolytes.

68yo female with relapsed multiple myeloma. Complaining of severe lower back pain and "fogginess." Labs show hypercalcemia (11.8 mg/dL) and increased M-protein spike. Cr is 1.6 mg/dL. BP 138/86. Skeletal survey reveals new lytic lesions in the L2-L3 vertebrae. Rx: Start Daratumumab/Bortezomib/Dexamethasone (DRd) regimen. Administer Zoledronic acid 4mg IV today (dose adjusted for renal function). Increase fluid intake to 2-3L per day. F/u in 1 week for repeat labs and pain assessment.

54yo male presents for first-time evaluation of change in bowel habits. Reports "pencil-thin" stools and occasional bright red blood per rectum for 2 months. Denies family history of CRC. On DRE, a firm, palpable mass is felt 5cm from the anal verge. Hgb is 10.8 g/dL (baseline 14.5). Vitals: BP 128/82, HR 76. Referred for urgent colonoscopy and pelvic MRI. Rx: Ferrous sulfate 325mg daily for iron deficiency. Pt advised to avoid NSAIDs until after GI eval.

57yo female, G2P2, post-menopausal, with Stage IIIC high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma. Currently on Cycle 4 of Carboplatin/Paclitaxel. Reports significant peripheral neuropathy in toes and fingers (Grade 2). BP 118/74, HR 80. CA-125 has decreased from 450 to 65. Physical exam shows decreasing abdominal distention/ascites. Rx: Gabapentin 300mg TID for neuropathy. Reduce Paclitaxel dose by 20% for next cycle. F/u for mid-treatment CT scan next week.

74yo male with Gleason 4+3=7 adenocarcinoma of the prostate. Status post-prostatectomy 2 years ago, now presenting with a rising PSA (currently 1.2 ng/mL, previously undetectable). Bone scan negative, but Axumin PET shows localized recurrence in the prostatic bed. BP 140/88. Patient asymptomatic. Rx: Begin Bicalutamide 500mg daily followed by Leuprolide injection. Refer to Radiation Oncology for salvage radiotherapy. PSA to be checked in 3 months.

39yo female presents with a changing mole on the right posterior calf. Pt reports the lesion has darkened and the borders have become irregular over the last 6 months. It occasionally itches but hasn't bled. On exam, 8mm asymmetrical macule with variegated colors (black/blue). No palpable popliteal or inguinal adenopathy. Vitals WNL. Performed a 2mm punch biopsy today. Rx: Topical bacitracin to biopsy site. Pt will be called with pathology results to determine if a wide local excision is required.

66yo male with history of Barrett's esophagus presents with progressive dysphagia, now limited to liquids only. 10lb weight loss. BP 115/70, HR 82. Endoscopy shows a circumferential mass in the distal esophagus. Biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. CT shows no distant metastases but enlarged mediastinal nodes. Rx: Start daily Famotidine 20mg. Refer for placement of jejunostomy tube for nutritional support. Plan for concurrent chemoradiation (Carboplatin/Paclitaxel) prior to surgical consult.

63yo female with recurrent non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC). History of smoking (quit 5 years ago). Presents for routine surveillance cystoscopy. Small papillary lesion noted near the right ureteral orifice. BP 134/76. Urine cytology positive for high-grade urothelial cells. Rx: Scheduled for TURBT (Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumor) on Thursday. Will follow with intravesical BCG induction (6 weekly treatments). Continue oxybutynin 5mg QD for bladder spasms.

16yo male presents with persistent right knee pain for 4 weeks, originally attributed to a sports injury. Pain is worse at night and does not respond to rest. Exam shows localized swelling and warmth over the distal femur. No joint instability. Vitals: BP 112/68, HR 84. X-ray shows a "sunburst" periosteal reaction and a Codman triangle at the distal femoral metaphysis. Highly suspicious for Osteosarcoma. Rx: Naproxen 500mg BID. Urgent referral to Orthopedic Oncology for biopsy and staging CT/PET.

45yo male in chronic phase CML, on Imatinib for 3 years. Presents for routine molecular monitoring. Pt reports good adherence but mentions occasional muscle cramps. Vitals: BP 122/80, HR 70. Spleen is not palpable. BCR-ABL1 transcript level is 0.008% (Major Molecular Response). Labs show mild neutropenia (ANC 1.2) but stable. Rx: Continue Imatinib 400mg QD. Calcium/Magnesium supplement for cramps. F/u in 3 months for repeat PCR.

31yo female with a palpable thyroid nodule found during routine physical. Ultrasound shows a 1.8cm hypoechoic nodule with microcalcifications in the right lobe. FNA confirmed Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (Bethesda VI). BP 110/72, HR 68. Thyroid function tests (TSH/T4) are normal. Discussed total thyroidectomy vs. lobectomy. Rx: No meds pre-op. Scheduled for total thyroidectomy and central neck dissection next month. Pt educated on lifelong Levothyroxine requirement post-op.

67yo male with Child-Pugh Class B cirrhosis and a 5cm HCC in the right lobe. Not a candidate for resection due to portal hypertension. BP 112/64, HR 78. AFP is 850 ng/mL. CT shows no extrahepatic spread. Discussed TACE (Transarterial Chemoembolization) as a bridge to transplant evaluation. Rx: Spironolactone 100mg QD, Nadolol 20mg QD. Refer to Hepatobiliary surgery and Transplant coordinator. Scheduled for TACE procedure in 10 days.

62yo female presents with post-menopausal bleeding. Menopause occurred at age 51. Pt has BMI of 34 and history of HTN. BP 150/92, HR 80. Pelvic US shows endometrial thickness of 12mm. Endometrial biopsy performed in office today. Rx: Lisinopril 10mg daily (restart for BP control). Pt to return in 1 week for path results. If malignant, will proceed with staging laparoscopy and total hysterectomy/bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.
